references.text: The Levites were appointed to serve at the tabernacle and care for holy things. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, it is ironic that a Levite—one set apart for religious service—passed by the injured man without helping.

The tribe of Levi was presented before Aaron the priest to serve him and minister at the tabernacle. The Levite in Jesus' parable thus had a special calling to serve God and the people, making his indifference in the story all the more striking.
In 2 Chronicles it is noted that the Levites were sometimes more sincere in heart than the priests. Yet in Luke 10:32, the Levite fails to act with mercy despite his religious role.

The priest in the previous verse (Luke 10:31) behaves in exactly the same way as the Levite—both see the injured man and pass by on the other side. The expression 'ὁμοίως' (likewise) directly links the Levite's action to that of the priest.

In contrast to both the priest and the Levite who passed by, the Samaritan stops, shows compassion, and actively cares for the injured man. The Samaritan's actions highlight the criticism of the religious leaders' lack of mercy.
Hosea 6:6 emphasizes that God desires mercy, not sacrifice. The Levite's neglect in the parable illustrates precisely this prioritization of outward religiosity over true compassion.
Micah 6:8 calls people to do what is right, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. The Levite in the parable fails this very call by passing by the one in need.

Priests and Levites were sent from Jerusalem to question John the Baptist. This shows that priests and Levites still held active religious authority in Jesus' time, making the Levite's failure in the parable even more blameworthy.

James emphasizes that faith without works is dead—seeing a brother in need and merely saying 'go in peace' without helping is worthless. The Levite's behavior in Luke 10:32 is a practical example of this empty piety.
